units.en: Variables have a unique way for applying colouring, also allowing extra formatting characters. These are applied after a pipe placed at the end of the variable's name, such as ⟦0⟧ that will turn the colour of the variable ⟦1⟧ red. If no colouring is applied, it will use the same colour as regular text: the §-colour block, textbox's ⟦2⟧, or the font's default colour in that order.
The list of formatting characters that are restricted to variables only are the following:
Converts the variable to SI units—appends "K" or "M" and divides the variable appropriately, such as 65 536 becoming 65.53K and 1 500 000 becoming 1.50M. Displays 2 decimals after the dot by default.
Prefixes the variable with ⟦0⟧ if the value is positive or ⟦1⟧ if it is negative.

Controls the number of decimals to display. Due to the nature of the game's variables, there are no more than 5 decimals that can be shown. Using any digit greater than 5 will instead have the same result as 5.
Converts the variable to percentage, multiplying by 100 and appending a %. By default, will show 2 digits after the decimal point, though the second digit will always be 0.
Appends a percentage to the end of the variable without multiplying by 100.
Colours the variable green if positive, yellow if zero, red if negative.
Colours the variable red if positive, yellow if zero, green if negative.

Any unrecognised symbols will neither change how the variable is localised nor get recognised as an error in-game. For example, it's common practice in the base game to prepend a dot before the digit used to control the amount of displayed digits as ⟦0⟧. In case of overlap between mutually-exclusive rules, the last-used one will be prioritised. However, static colouring has a lower priority than dynamic colouring (e.g. ⟦1⟧ will be treated as ⟦2⟧), and using ⟦3⟧ will also override ⟦4⟧.
Some examples of formatting characters in usage:

Within these examples, the first string depicts the current scope's democratic popularity as a percentage multiplied by 100 (%), in green (G), rounded to a whole number with 0 decimals (0). The second string displays the ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧'s value as a 'good' number (+ making it green if positive, red if negative), with a percentage sign appended in the end (%%) and rounded to a number with one decimal (.1). The third string displays the variable in yellow colouring (as is common in the base game's tooltips), leaving it unchanged otherwise.

By default, variable-related arguments such as ⟦0⟧ or ⟦1⟧ do not have a tooltip. For ⟦2⟧ of these arguments, such as ⟦3⟧, it is possible to set a tooltip with an optional ⟦4⟧ argument within. Others, such as ⟦5⟧, do not support this and a custom tooltip must be used instead, whether it's for ⟦6⟧ or for ⟦7⟧.

This tooltip argument is notable since the value of that localisation key allows using two ⟦0⟧ marked with dollar signs: ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧. ⟦3⟧ represents the variable's value before the operation, while ⟦4⟧ represents the variable's value after the operation. This can be used to let the player know the current and/or the potential value of the variable in the same localisation key without taking up more space with ⟦5⟧.
Here's an example of it being done:
This is the effect itself. Within localisation, this would be done:

By default, an unset variable is equal to zero when checked. However, the game also provides a null coalescing operator for variables, used with a question mark. For example, ⟦0⟧ within a decision will result in the cost of the decision being the same as var_name for the country. However, if that variable was never set or was cleared beforehand, then the decision will cost 100 ⟦1⟧ instead of 0.

Similarly to flags, a variable can be set as targeted by appending the target with ⟦0⟧. However, there are differences: in variables this does not append the target's ID to the name but stores it as a separate variable, as well as it being possible to target far more than countries, but also, for example, states or ideology groups. A variable reference ⟦1⟧ would resolve to a variable named ⟦2⟧. If called in a scope where PREV⟦3⟧, a variable reference ⟦4⟧ would resolve to a variable named ⟦5⟧. This can even be applied to temporary variables. You can also target variables using the syntax ⟦6⟧, regardless of the type of their value: be it country, state, token, even a raw integer. Variables targeting tokenizable types such as ideology groups and ideas provides a powerful alternative to scoped variables for associating a set of variable fields together, enabling one to get around the fact that ideas, ideologies, etc. do not have their own scopes. Generally, when you target a token, it is pasted in as its underlying integer ID (a number in the ten-thousands, usually), but this generally works fine, because it's consistent; the only problem is it's not human-readable. In general, variable targeting is substantially more optimized than meta-effect/trigger token pasting, not to mention more readable and understandable, so should be preferred wherever feasible.

It is technically possible, under some circumstances, to use multiple target specifiers in one variable name, usually strung together back-to-back at the end of the name, like ⟦0⟧. However, this is extremely inconsistent, and the exact rules that govern how it behaves are currently an open question.

The following is a list of variable-related effects and triggers. Variable-modifying effects have an equivalent for temporary variables, with ⟦0⟧ being used instead of ⟦1⟧, and these temporary variable operators are also valid triggers, as described above. Every operator can be used with variables that do not exist, assuming a value of 0 unless a null-coalescing operator is used.
⟦0⟧ The variable to modify or create. value = <decimal>/<variable> The value to set the variable to. tooltip = localisation_keyLocalisation used by the operation. Optional.
set_variable = { var = my_variable value = 100 tooltip = set_var_to_100_tt } set_temp_variable = { temp_var = ROOT.overlord }
Sets a variable's value to the specified amount, creating it if not defined.

⟦0⟧ The variable to modify or create. min = <decimal> The minimum possible value, defaults to 0. max = <decimal> The maximum possible value, defaults to 1. integer = <bool> Sets if the variable must be an integer or if it can be decimal. Defaults to false.
set_variable_to_random = { var = random_num max = 11 integer = yes } set_temp_variable_to_random = my_var
Sets a variable's value to the specified amount, creating it if not defined. The result will be greater than or equal than the minimum and strictly less than the maximum.
Shortened version exists with ⟦0⟧, setting it to a decimal between 0 and 1. Can be used in triggers.
Clears the value from the memory entirely.
Can only be used on regular variables.

⟦0⟧ Variable to compare. value = <decimal>/<variable> The value to compare the variable to. compare = <compare type>/<variable> The comparison type. Variants are equals, not_equals, less_than, less_than_or_equals, greater_than, and greater_than_or_equals. Defaults to greater_than_or_equals.
check_variable = { var = my_var value = 10 compare = greater_than_or_equals } check_variable = { var_name > 10 }
Compares the value of a variable. Used as a trigger.

Temporary and regular formatting use the exact same formatting. Shortened variant exists as ⟦0⟧, where the operator in the middle is an equality sign (=), greater than sign (>), or a lesser than sign (<). The comparison type is always strict in this case: ⟦1⟧ will come up as false if ⟦2⟧ is exactly 10.
Checks if the value was set, regardless of its amount. Used as a trigger.
A variable is considered set even if its value is 0, as long as it wasn't cleared.
⟦0⟧ The variable to add to. value = <decimal>/<variable> The value to add to the variable. tooltip = localisation_keyLocalisation used by the operation. Optional.
add_to_variable = { var = my_variable value = 100 tooltip = add_100_to_var_tt } add_to_temp_variable = { temp_var = num_owned_states }
Increases a variable's value by the specified amount, creating it if not defined.
⟦0⟧ The variable to subtract from. value = <decimal>/<variable> The value to subtract from the variable. tooltip = localisation_keyLocalisation used by the operation. Optional.
subtract_from_variable = { var = my_variable value = 100 tooltip = sub_100_from_var_tt } subtract_from_temp_variable = { temp_var = num_owned_states }
Decreases a variable's value by the specified amount, creating it if not defined.
Shortened version exists with ⟦0⟧. Equivalent to adding a negative amount.
⟦0⟧ The variable to multiply. value = <decimal>/<variable> The value to multiply the variable by. tooltip = localisation_keyLocalisation used by the operation. Optional.
multiply_variable = { var = my_variable value = 100 tooltip = multiply_var_by_100_tt } multiply_temp_variable = { temp_var = num_owned_states }
Multiplies a variable's value by the specified amount.
⟦0⟧ The variable to divide. value = <decimal>/<variable> The value to divide the variable by. tooltip = localisation_keyLocalisation used by the operation. Optional.
divide_variable = { var = my_variable value = 100 tooltip = divide_var_by_100_tt } divide_temp_variable = { temp_var = num_owned_states }
Divides a variable's value by the specified amount.
⟦0⟧ The variable to modulo. value = <decimal>/<variable> The value to modulo the variable by. tooltip = localisation_keyLocalisation used by the operation. Optional.
modulo_variable = { var = my_variable value = 50 tooltip = get_modulo_of_var_by_50_tt } modulo_temp_variable = { temp_var = num_controlled_states }
Makes the variable become the remainder of Euclidean division of the variable by the specified value.
Rounds the variable towards the closest integer value.
If exactly between two integers (Such as 1.5), the option with lager absolute val gets chosen ( if -1.5,will be -2 ).
⟦0⟧ The variable to clamp. min = <decimal>/<variable> The minimum value of the variable after the clamp. max = <decimal>/<variable> The maximum value of the variable after the clamp.
clamp_variable = { var = my_var min = 0 } clamp_temp_variable = { var = my_var min = 0 }
Clamps the variable to ensure its value is between the two specified numbers, raising to the minimum if smaller or lowering to the maximum if larger.

Either min or max can be omitted, in which case it'll not be checked. Does nothing if the variable is already in the range between min and max. ⟦0⟧, it can still go beyond the minimum or the maximum after the clamp.
This only changes the current value of the variable
⟦0⟧ The variable to modify or create. value = <decimal>/<variable> The value to set the variable to.
Sets a temporary variable to a value or another variable.
Calculations with extensive number of steps and complex usage of temporary variables may be simplified with the usage of math expressions.

Returns 1 if the accumulator is less than the value, otherwise 0.
Returns 1 if the accumulator is greater than the value, otherwise 0.
Adds a value to the accumulator.
Returns 1 if both the accumulator and the value are non-zero, otherwise 0.

Sets the accumulator to the quadrant-aware arctangent atan2(y, x), where the accumulator is y and the value is x. The result is expressed in radians.

This is computed with a numerical approximation and may be off by a few hundredths of a radian; follow with ⟦0⟧ if you need an exact result. The degenerate case atan2(0, 0) returns roughly pi/2 rather than 0.
